opus-5.5.text:
It's a really natural idea, and I think a lot of people, myself included, were drawn to it after AlphaGo. PUCT works beautifully in Go because of a few properties that are worth spelling out: the action space is discrete and fairly small, around a few hundred legal moves; you have a perfect simulator, so you know exactly what state results from each move; and the value function gets a clean terminal signal of win or loss. The policy prior narrows the branching, the value network lets you truncate rollouts, and the visit counts give you a much sharper training target than the raw policy. That loop of search producing better targets, then distilling them back into the network, is the real magic.

When you try to port that to LLM reasoning, several of those assumptions break. First, what counts as an "action"? If it's a token, the tree is absurdly deep and most branches differ trivially, so you burn compute exploring "the" versus "a." If it's a sentence or a reasoning step, you've got a continuous, effectively infinite space, and you have to sample candidates, which means your branching is only as good as your sampler's diversity. Second, the value function is much harder. In Go you can tell fairly reliably who's winning midgame. In a proof or a coding problem, partial reasoning traces are hard to score; a step can look plausible and be fatally wrong, or look awkward and be exactly right. Process reward models try to fill that gap, but they're noisy and very exploitable, and search is precisely the thing that finds the exploits in your value model.

Third, and this is the part I find most interesting, language models already do a kind of implicit search inside a single chain of thought. They backtrack, they say "wait, that's wrong," they try another approach. So the empirical story so far has been that just doing RL on long chains of thought with verifiable rewards gets you most of the benefit you'd hoped explicit tree search would give, and it's much simpler and scales better on current hardware. Sequential sampling turns out to be a decent substitute for branching when the model can condition on its own past mistakes, which a Go engine's nodes can't do.

That said, I don't think tree search is dead. Where you have a cheap, reliable verifier, like formal math in Lean, or unit tests in code, the Go-like conditions come back: you get a crisp terminal reward, and search over proof steps can work really well. And the deeper lesson of AlphaZero, using search as a policy improvement operator and distilling it back, still seems right to me. I'd just expect the winning version to look less like literal PUCT over tokens and more like the model learning to allocate its own exploration, with explicit search reserved for domains where you can actually check your answers.

r001.rationale: The response says token-level search is excessively deep and wastes compute on trivial branches, but it does not identify excessive greediness over local token choices as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It says partial reasoning can look plausible yet be fatally wrong, but does not state that correct intermediate thoughts may fail to help solve the ultimate problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I'm a bit of a skeptic on this one, and I'll try to explain why.

The reason PUCT worked so beautifully for Go is that Go gives you three things for free that language doesn't. First, the action space is small and discrete: at most a few hundred legal moves, and the policy prior can put real mass on the good ones. Second, you have a perfect simulator. You can roll the board forward and the state you land in is exactly the state you'd get in the real game. And third, you have a clean terminal reward. Someone wins. The value network is being trained toward a ground truth signal that's dense enough, after enough games, to actually be calibrated.

When you move to LLM reasoning, every one of those breaks a little. The branching factor is the vocabulary, or if you chunk at the level of "thoughts," it's effectively unbounded, so the prior does almost all the work and search is doing cleanup. The "simulator" is the model itself, so rolling forward doesn't give you new information about the world, it gives you more samples from your own belief. And for most interesting problems, the reward is either sparse, like a math problem with a verifier, or it's a learned reward model that is exactly the thing an adversarial search will exploit. Tree search is a very good optimizer, and if the thing it optimizes is a proxy, you get the proxy, not the thing.

That said, I don't think it's hopeless, I just think the Go analogy is the wrong mental model. Where I've seen search-like things actually help is narrow: code and math, where you have an external verifier, and the search is really just "sample a lot, prune with a checker." That's closer to best-of-N with a decent value estimate than it is to deep lookahead. In Go, the depth of search was the point, because tactics compound over twenty moves. In reasoning, the equivalent of that depth is mostly already baked into the forward pass or the chain of thought. The model is doing a kind of amortized search every time it generates.

The other thing I'd flag is the compute trade-off. Any FLOPs you spend on test-time search are FLOPs you could have spent on training, and historically in deep learning, putting the compute into the weights has tended to win over putting it into inference-time procedure. AlphaGo Zero is the counterexample people cite, but note what happened there: search was used as a training-time policy improvement operator, and then distilled back into the network. The lesson I take is "use search to generate better targets," not "run search at inference forever." If I were betting, that's where PUCT-style ideas land for LLMs: in the data flywheel, generating and filtering trajectories, rather than as the thing running when you hit send.

So short version: as a training-time tool with a real verifier, promising. As a general inference-time reasoning engine on open-ended tasks, I'd expect it to be outcompeted by just training a better model, and I'd watch very carefully for it finding holes in the reward instead of finding answers.

r001.rationale: The response notes that the prior may dominate search, but it does not identify excessive greediness over local token choices as a limitation.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that individually correct intermediate thoughts may fail to help solve the overall problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what makes search work so well in Go, and do we have those ingredients for language? In Go, you have a precise transition function, a relatively manageable action space, and an unambiguous outcome. You can play a game to the end and know who won. That gives you a way to train a value function, which then makes your search more effective.

With language, you can certainly build a tree of possible continuations and use PUCT to allocate compute. But what’s the value of an intermediate paragraph? If your evaluator has some systematic misconception, searching harder might just find an answer that exploits that misconception. You need something that grounds the evaluation.

That’s why I’m more excited about this in domains like programming or math, where you can run a test or check a proof. There, search can produce verified solutions, and those solutions can improve the model, which makes subsequent search better. That feedback loop is very powerful.

I’m less convinced that the right unit of search is an individual token. You might want to branch over an entire approach: try this decomposition, write this program, introduce this lemma. So I’m optimistic about search as a way to spend more compute on difficult problems. I’m more uncertain that taking the exact machinery that worked for Go and applying it to a token tree is the best implementation.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether individual tokens are the right search unit, but does not identify excessive greediness over local token choices as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It questions how to evaluate an intermediate paragraph, but does not state that a correct intermediate thought may fail to help solve the overall problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what do you get to use as your verifier? In Go, you have a perfect simulator. You can take an action, advance the board, and eventually find out whether you won. You also have a pretty well-defined action space. With language, neither of those things is quite as clean.

You can certainly treat a chunk of reasoning as an action and build a search tree over those chunks. The language model gives you a prior, and you could train a value function to predict which branches are promising. But if that value function is just another model judging whether something sounds right, search can end up exploiting its mistakes. You get a very convincing argument that’s wrong.

I’m more optimistic in domains where you can actually check the result—code, for example, where you can run tests. Then spending more compute exploring different approaches has a clear feedback signal. The interesting question is whether you can take those successful searches and distill them back into the model, so that something that initially required a lot of exploration becomes something the model can do directly.

So I think search is a promising ingredient. I’m less sure that the specific machinery of PUCT is the important part. You need a useful way to propose alternatives, evaluate them, and learn from the computation you spent.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using the language model’s prior to propose reasoning chunks, but does not identify excessive greediness over local token choices as a limitation of PUCT.

r002.rationale: The response warns that a value model may favor convincing but wrong arguments. It does not say PUCT can yield correct intermediate thoughts that fail to help solve the ultimate problem.
